why: Met object page gives Lydian, ca. 560-546 BCE, 8.087 g, 1 x 1.6 x 0.3 cm; single source but it is the catalogue record itself (also: excavated at Sardis 13 April 1922).

fix: Electrum is a natural gold-silver alloy, and Lydian electrum coins appeared in the late seventh century BCE, though the exact date is disputed.
why: Met says 'apparently ... end of the seventh century' and 'exact date ... in dispute'; CEPR says around 630 BCE; the claim should carry the hedge.

Live Science: varying ratio made value unpredictable; CEPR: neither weighing nor touchstone gives the percentage precisely (CEPR alone for touchstone; both popular/secondary; royal Sardis electrum was steady ~55% gold).
Sardis Expedition: refinery near the Pactolus, used in first half of 6th c. BC; BMCR's Ramage date ca. 575-550 BC is consistent.

Greenewalt: electrum layered with salt in coarse pottery containers, heated in ovens, silver converted to silver chloride, gold 'basically pure'; BMCR agrees (lidded earthenware pot, 600-800 C). Harvard Magazine supports salt parting but not ovens.

fix: According to the Sardis Expedition, the Sardis furnaces and parting vessels are the earliest known archaeological evidence for the cementation process anywhere.
why: One source only; Harvard Magazine says only 'not found elsewhere' and BMCR notes gold purification processes were known long before Sardis, so attribute it and say 'archaeological'.

fix: Croesus, traditionally dated c. 560-546 BCE, is commonly (though not unanimously) credited with issuing the first coins of pure gold and pure silver, which appeared shortly before the middle of the sixth century BCE.
why: Attribution supported but disputed (BMCR 'not unanimously'); reign dates also disputed: Hesperia 2025 supports Wallace's view that Croesus's reign began in the 580s; Live Science gives 547 as end date.

fix: Both the gold and silver Croeseids carried the confronted foreparts of a lion and a bull; one source says the dies for gold and silver were interchangeable.
why: Lion-bull design on both metals well supported (Met, Ashmolean, Sardis); interchangeable dies only on the Colorado page (John Nebel), from a single illustrated example.

fix: Heavy Croeseid gold and silver staters weighed about 10.7-10.9 g; the standard was later reduced to light gold staters of about 8.2 g and silver coins (sigloi) of about 5.3-5.4 g.
why: Colorado gives 10.9 g heavy and 8.2/5.4 g light ('concurrently (and later on)', not a clean replacement); Live Science gives 10.7 g; Ashmolean/Harvard silver pieces 5.33/5.31 g. Met coin 8.087 g is light class, which Colorado thinks may be Persian-era.

fix: The reverse of a Croeseid stater carries two incuse square punches, on gold and silver alike.
why: Live Science's 'one on silver' is contradicted: Sardis Expedition, Ashmolean and Harvard silver croeseids all list two incuse punches; Met page does not describe 26.59.2's reverse.

Colorado page (John Nebel) reports Vickers 1985 (Darius), Root 1988 refutation and its Croesus conclusion; Hesperia 2025 independently finds silver croeseids in the 547 BCE destruction level. Debate details rest on one secondary page.
Lexundria Macaulay text matches the quote exactly; Met only paraphrases. Herodotus's claim is his own; modern dating of first coinage is disputed.
